pr_title: Use ASN1_TIME for handling time comparisons in ca.c:do_updatedb
pr_body:
Fixes #13944
   + changed ASN1_UTCTIME to ASN1_TIME
   + removed all Y2K code from do_updatedb
   + changed compare to ASN1_TIME_compare
pr_comments:
I made manual tests:
- The certificate that I mentioned in the bug is handled properly
- Certificates in the near future are handled properly
- Certificates in the near past are handled properly
I do not have any certificates available having expired long ago, especially not before 2000-01-01.
I also checked whether there is a testing infrastructure available to add tests, but I didn't find any - at least not in the 1.1.1 branch.
Please fix the possible leaks and I'll approve.

Ok, I'll have a look at the leaks - can't promise how fast.
About the testing: I there a testing infrastructure in the master branch? Having tests is certainly a good idea but I doubt I could build up an infrastructure being consistent to the rest of openssl.

> Ok, I'll have a look at the leaks - can't promise how fast.
> About the testing: I there a testing infrastructure in the master branch? Having tests is certainly a good idea but I doubt I could build up an infrastructure being consistent to the rest of openssl.

In master there are already various tests for the ca application in `test/recipes/80-test_ca.t`. However there is no test involving the `-updatedb` option.

> > Ok, I'll have a look at the leaks - can't promise how fast.
> > About the testing: I there a testing infrastructure in the master branch? Having tests is certainly a good idea but I doubt I could build up an infrastructure being consistent to the rest of openssl.
> 
> In master there are already various tests for the ca application in `test/recipes/80-test_ca.t`. However there is no test involving the `-updatedb` option.

I had a look at this infrastructure and I see a major blocker to write tests for it:
I would need to modify "now". My idea is to:

1. Create a very long running CA in the past (I would create one before Y2K).
2. Create some certificates with relevant test values (expiration < Y2K, expiration > Y2K, expiration 2049, expiration >= 2050).
3. Run updatedb on dates in the times between two expiration dates. I would make a whole testrun for each time gap (to ensure also the correct expiration for the certificate expired < Y2K when the first updatedb is calles > 2050) as well as a series of updatedbs.

Any ideas how I could realize this? I never wrote tests in C where I had to override the system time, perhaps there is a simple way I don't know?
The `ca` command takes `-startdate` and `-enddate` flags, will that not be good enough?

> The `ca` command takes `-startdate` and `-enddate` flags, will that not be good enough?

I don't think so, because I need to manipulate the system time when running the `updatedb` command. Do `startdate` and `enddate` allow values in the past?

> I don't think so, because I need to manipulate the system time when running the updatedb command. Do startdate and enddate allow values in the past?

Yes.  Note that this is only for certs, not other commands.

> > I don't think so, because I need to manipulate the system time when running the updatedb command. Do startdate and enddate allow values in the past?
> 
> Yes. Note that this is only for certs, not other commands.

So one solution could be to introduce a parameter to specify the date `updatedb` should use instead of the current time. And since `-startdate` and `-enddate` are not working for the CA itself, this would also have to be introduced. Would this be an acceptable solution or is this change to deep?
BTW: Is this PR the best place for this discussion?
I do not think it is worth it. The parameter would be useful only for testing.
This pull request is ready to merge

> I do not think it is worth it. The parameter would be useful only for testing.

I was thinking about different approaches. One idea was to call the CA commands with fake system times. In Linux (and probably most supported Unix-like systems), this could be achieved relatively easy using the "faketime" command. I have no idea (and it's close to impossible for me to test that) whether it's possible to compile this for Windows.
The second issue coming to my mind is, that this would introduce an external dependency for building openssl.
On the other hand: having automated tests for code at least running on some platforms is already an advantage to having none at all.
Alternatively we could move the logic into a library, and modify the existing ca.c to contain as little logic as possible and create an additional command (ca_test.c) where we could add code like fake times we need for tests.
Any ideas about these thoughts?

> Alternatively we could move the logic into a library, and modify the existing ca.c to contain as little logic as possible and create an additional command (ca_test.c) where we could add code like fake times we need for tests.

With 3.0 this is doable. The ca_test could even live in the test subdirectory and link that library (well, it does not have to be a library, just refactored out c file that would contain the common parts of the code between the test and the ca application). Look at how cmp_client_test is built in the test/build.info

I am going to merge this PR. If you want to add the test in master, you're welcome. Please open a new PR for that.
Merged to master and 1.1.1 branch. Thank you for the contribution!

Look at how cmp_client_test is built in the test/build.info

> I am going to merge this PR. If you want to add the test in master, you're welcome. Please open a new PR for that.

This was my plan anyway. If I really make relevant progress there, is there a way to get feedback for PoC or support for specific questions (best practices in openssl) without starting a PR? I dislike the idea of opening a PR when knowing in advance it is far from being really productive...

PRs are quite cheap and are the best way to review even the PoC. Do not worry about opening it. You can also always force push a completely new code to the PoC PR branch if you need to start from scratch. You do not have to create a new branch and new PR in that case.
If you have just a question, no real code to commit, please open an issue of the question type.

issue_context.title: updatedb expires certificates with expiration date having 4-digit years before 2100.
issue_context.body: In a private CA, I have some very long running certificates. In index.txt one of the expiration dates is 20730104163541Z meaning the certificate is valid until early 2073. If I run an updatedb command on this CA, this certificate is marked as "expired". I assume this is, because only the first two digits are interpreted as a year and this certificate therefore looks as if it would have been expired in 2020. I'm using openssl 1.1.1d.
comments:
There does seem to be some dubious Y2K handling going on here, which could be the cause:

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/c9603dfa42d0643a6c8cac3e14364d9fd63303c4/apps/ca.c#L2290-L2322

I think the problem starts earlier: The current time is stored in an ASN1_UTCTIME which - according to the man pages - is limited to a year range of 1950 through 2049. This explains, why in lines 2290 - 2293 only the first two digits are used to detect whether current time is before Y2k or after Y2k. However this will be fixed, this is not the current problem - not solving it will cause major trouble in 29 years...
The current error starts in line 2300. From the database, there are also used the first two digits to detect before Y2k or after Y2k. For dates starting from 2050, the result is always "20", assuming year 2020, which explains, why this issue becomes visible now.
As a first fix, there needs to be a check whether the timestamp in the database is stored with 2 digits or with 4 digits. If it is stored with 4 digits, it always has to be after Y2k.
After this is fixed, the strcmp in line 2307 will cause trouble, because it assumes the same amount of digits for years on both sides. A first fix could be to remove the first two digits of the year from the database string if it has a 4 digit year, then the strcmp in line 2307 will work properly again.

I tried to implement my idea described above and I could fix this issue. Since I don't have a permission to create a branch in the repo, I cannot create a pull request for this. I created a classic patch file and attach it here. Perhaps someone can check my suggested solution...
[issue-13944.patch.txt](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/files/5890379/issue-13944.patch.txt)

You have to fork the repo to your personal github account first. Then you clone the fork, do the work there (preferably in a new branch) and then create the PR against the master branchm of the parent openssl repo.
